title: St John's wort infused oil for nerve pain
subtitle: A red-pigmented oil for neuralgia, bruising, and nerve injury
excerpt: St John's wort flowers steeped in olive oil for four to six weeks until the oil runs a deep, distinctive red. Traditionally applied externally for nerve pain, neuralgia, and bruising. Makes about 200 ml. The drug-interaction profile of St John's wort applies even to this external preparation, so read the safety notes before you start.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931) : Hypericum perforatum entry, the red oil preparation. King's American Dispensatory (Felter and Lloyd, 1898) : Hypericum, external applications for nerve injury. EMA HMPC monograph on Hypericum perforatum (2009) : safety assessment including photosensitivity and drug-interaction profile. British Herbal Pharmacopoeia (1983) : Hypericum perforatum, external preparations.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The cool-infuse path takes 4 to 6 weeks. Start the oil when the flowers are freshly dried. Keeps 12 months in dark glass.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Store in a cool, dark cupboard in amber glass. Discard if the oil smells rancid, or if the red colour fades to a pale straw yellow (the hypericin pigment has degraded).

recipeTools.notes: Optional: for the warm-infuse method instead of the cool solar infuse
Required only if using the warm-infuse method

glossaryTerms.definition: A carrier oil that has been gently heated or cold-infused with dried plant material to draw out fat-soluble constituents. Different from an essential oil, which is a steam-distilled concentrate.

A slow, cool method of infusing plant material into oil using natural warmth from a sunny windowsill over four to six weeks. The plant releases its constituents gradually into the oil without the use of heat.

projectSchedule.title: Start your oil
projectSchedule.body: Pack the dried St John's wort flowers into a clean maceration jar. Pour over the olive oil until the herb is fully submerged with at least 2 cm of oil above. Seal the jar and place it in a sunny windowsill. Label with today's date.

projectSchedule.title: Check for condensation
projectSchedule.body: Look inside the jar. There should be no visible moisture or cloudy water droplets. If the jar has been in a very cold window at night and warmed in the day, condensation can form on the glass : tip the jar gently to check the oil is still clear and the herb is still submerged. Top up with a little more olive oil if needed.

projectSchedule.title: Check the colour and smell
projectSchedule.body: Tilt the jar and look at the oil. By now it should be turning a noticeable red or deep pink from the hypericin in the flowers. Smell it: it should have a strong, slightly resinous, herbaceous scent. If the colour is still pale straw, give it another week or two. If it smells rancid or sour, the batch has failed and should be discarded.

projectSchedule.title: Strain and bottle your oil
projectSchedule.body: Your oil is ready to strain and bottle. Line a sieve with a double layer of muslin over a clean jug. Pour the oil through and press the spent herb to extract the last of the oil. The strained oil should be a rich, jewel-like red. Funnel into clean amber glass bottles, label, and store in a cool dark cupboard.

content.text: St John's wort infused oil is dried flowers steeped in olive oil over four to six weeks until the oil turns a deep, characteristic red. That red colour comes from the hypericin-rich active compounds in the flowers, and it is the clearest sign the infusion has worked. This is an external preparation, applied to the skin over areas of nerve pain, neuralgia, or bruising. Traditionally used in western herbal practice for nerve injury and mild bruising. The preparation takes patience: the
solar infusion
path runs four to six weeks on a sunny windowsill. A warm double-boiler method will finish in two to four hours but the slow path is traditionally preferred for this herb. The finished
infused oil
keeps 12 months in a dark glass bottle.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms. This preparation is for external use only. St John's wort is a potent inducer of the CYP3A4 liver enzyme and significantly lowers the blood level of many prescription drugs. Even in an external oil, absorption through the skin means readers on any of the following should consult their prescriber before using this preparation: SSRIs and SNRIs, hormonal contraceptives (the pill, the patch, the ring, the implant), warfarin, transplant immunosuppressants (ciclosporin, tacrolimus), HIV antiretrovirals, and many anti-cancer drugs. The interaction list is long and serious. Photosensitivity: topical St John's wort can sensitise the skin to sunlight. After applying the oil, do not expose the treated area to strong sun. Cover with clothing if you are going outdoors. Pregnancy: consult a herbalist or your midwife before using this remedy in pregnancy.

content.text: Ingredients

items.prepNote: dried flowers (not fresh; the moisture in fresh flowers encourages mould). The flowers should be a rich yellow when dried.
light or extra-light olive oil; any neutral, stable carrier oil works

content.text: Method: cool-infuse path (recommended)
Step 1: Pack the jar

Pack the dried flowers loosely into a clean, completely dry soaking period jar. Pour over the olive oil so the herb is fully submerged, with at least 2 cm of oil above the top of the herb. Any exposed herb will go mouldy. Seal the jar tightly. Label with the date.
Step 2: Place on a sunny windowsill

Put the jar in a south-facing window where it will get a few hours of sunlight each day. Tilt it gently once a day to keep the herb moving. Check every two weeks: look for colour change in the oil (it begins pale then shifts to pink, then to a rich red over four to six weeks), and check that there is no condensation or cloudiness inside the glass.
Step 3: Strain and bottle

After four to six weeks, when the oil is a good red, line a sieve with a double layer of muslin over a clean jug. Pour the oil through and press the spent herb firmly to extract everything. The finished oil should be a clear, deep red. Funnel into clean amber glass bottles, label with the date, and store in a cool dark cupboard.
Warm-infuse alternative

If you need the oil faster, use a double boiler. Set the flowers and oil in a heatproof bowl over simmering water. Keep the oil at 60 to 65 degrees Celsius using a probe thermometer and infuse for two to four hours, stirring occasionally. Strain and bottle as above. The colour will not be as deep red as the solar-infuse path, but the preparation is still effective.
How to use it

Warm a small amount between your palms and massage gently into the area of nerve pain or bruising. Do not apply to broken skin. After applying, keep the treated area covered if you are going outdoors into strong sunlight.
Dosing

Apply 2 to 4 ml (roughly half a teaspoon) to the affected area, up to three times a day. Massage in and leave to absorb. If there is no improvement after seven days of regular use, consult a doctor or herbalist rather than continuing.
Storage

Store in amber glass bottles in a cool, dark cupboard. Keeps 12 months from the strain date. Discard if the red colour fades significantly to a pale straw yellow (the active compounds have degraded), or if the oil smells rancid.
When not to use this remedy

Do not use if you are on any of the prescription medications listed in the safety notes above without first consulting your prescriber. Do not apply to broken skin or open wounds. Do not expose the treated area to strong sunlight after application. Do not use in pregnancy without advice from a herbalist or your midwife. See a doctor for nerve pain that is severe, worsening, spreading, or accompanied by weakness, numbness, or bladder or bowel changes.

attrs.heading: What went wrong
attrs.intro: Common problems with this preparation and how to avoid them.

items.symptom: The oil stayed pale straw yellow and never turned red
items.cause: Either the flowers were too old (stale dried herb over 12 months old loses its hypericin content). The jar did not get enough light, or the infusion time was too short.
items.fix: Use freshly dried flowers from the current season. Move the jar to a sunnier spot. Give it the full six weeks.

items.symptom: The oil went cloudy or has white flecks
items.cause: Moisture introduced either through the herb or condensation.
items.fix: Discard the batch. Ensure the herb is bone dry before packing, and that the jar and lid are completely dry.

items.symptom: The oil smells off or fermented
items.cause: Moisture, or the jar was stored somewhere too warm.
items.fix: Discard and start again. Keep the jar in a cool-ish bright window, not on a radiator shelf.
